subject: grayWolf
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: gray wolf standing alert.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning the proportions for a Warcraft-style gray wolf model, aiming for chunky exaggerated features like thick shoulders, big paws, and a heavy neck ruff with roughly 0.8m shoulder height and 1.4m body length.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: a hips root joint with spine, neck, tail, leg, head, jaw, and ear chains, laying out coordinates for a forward-facing wolf in an alert standing pose with head raised and ears up.

I'm extending the spine chain from rump to chest front so I can sweep the body mesh along it, tapering ellipse radii from narrower hips to a heavier, wider chest.

I'm defining the spine chain with a catmull path from hips upward, naming the joints spine1-3 with role "spine," and deciding the root hips joint can share that role too. Then I'm setting up the neck chain to parent off the last spine joint.

Working out the neck sweep from base to head with shrinking radii, planning thick Warcraft-style mane ruff using flattened cones scattered along the neck surface for fur tufts. Now I'm reasoning through how the head joint should attach at the neck's tip, oriented along the end tangent so it faces forward correctly.

For the skull shape, I'm sketching a wolf-style head: a boxy sphere skull, a tapered frustum muzzle, and a separate lower jaw on its own joint, all positioned using local forward/up/right offsets relative to the head joint.

I'll add a dark nose piece at the muzzle tip, plus small white fang cones on the upper and lower jaw for a slightly open, alert snarl pose. I'll pose the jaw bone with a small forward rotation (~6-8°) to open it just enough to reveal the fangs before building the rest of the jaw geometry.

Setting up the jaw joint off the head bone, positioned forward and slightly down, with the lower jaw built as a frustum extending from the joint to the chin tip using local coordinates along the jaw's orientation.

Now I'm placing the eyes for a fierce wolf look—amber glowing slanted eyes with dark slit pupils and angled brow ridges, positioned relative to the skull center, working out the ellipsoid surface math to get them sitting correctly on the skull's front curvature.

I'll slant the eye's long axis by spinning it about the normal, raising the outer corner for that fierce look — since fierce brows angle inward at the nose, the outer edge should tilt upward relative to the inner corner.

So mirrored spin convention: left eye positive, right eye negative, roughly consistent even if side-hit normals are approximate—good enough for this minor detail. For the pupil, I'll skip a separate flat box and instead use a small dark elliptical sphere embedded slightly lower, giving an amber glowing eye with a subtle slit pupil effect.

For the brow ridge, I'm adding a flattened, darker-colored wedge above each eye to suggest bone structure. For the ears, I'm shaping big pointed Warcraft-style triangles using an extruded outline positioned near the top of the head, angled slightly outward and tilted for that orc-like silhouette.

I'm placing the ear extrusion at the skull's base position with a darker inner-ear layer offset slightly forward, and considering whether to tilt the ears outward or keep them upright like a wolf's, leaning toward upright for a more classic look.

Working out the orthogonal basis vectors for the tilted ear geometry, then moving to plan cheek fur tufts — small spike cones attached near the head/skull joint, angled back and outward to form a ruff effect.

For the neck mane, I'm scattering spike cones across the neck's surface, blending the outward normal direction with a backward lean so each tuft sweeps back naturally like fur.

I'm keeping the spike geometry low-poly with fewer sides to manage part count, estimating around 400 total pieces across the model to stay under the limit—going with a Warcraft-style layered fur look: a dark mane ridge along the back and shoulders, lighter fluff at the chest, scattering roughly 45 spikes along the neck and front torso surfaces.

I'm defining the dorsal ridge spikes swept along the back path, a cream-white chest tuft cluster, and a bushy tail built from a tapering swept tube plus added tufts, with the tail chain hanging down and slightly back in an alert pose.

For coloring, I'm giving the tail a gradient fading from gray to near-black at the tip, and planning the overall coat with a countershading paint (dark gray-brown back, cream-white belly) plus a mottled texture for streaky fur.

Writing paint functions...

Writing coat shader logic...

Still writing coat shader logic...

Still refining muzzle blending, then moving to leg structure — thick Warcraft-style forelegs with shoulder-elbow-wrist-paw joints, working out root and target positions and segment lengths so the limb reaches the ground properly.

I'll build the leg chain with four named joints—shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw—using a polyline through manual points rather than a generic limb helper, keeping the tip joint aimed along the end tangent toward the toe.

Then I'm sweeping tubes along the chain with a tapering radius array from thick shoulder to thin toe, then adding an oversized paw cushion as a flattened ellipsoid with small toe spheres and dark claw cones to match the exaggerated stylized look.

I'm figuring out part counts per paw and then shifting to planning the hind leg joint positions (hip, knee, hock, paw) for the digitigrade stance.

I'm tapering the leg radius from thick at the hip down to narrow at the hock, adding a haunch mass for thigh muscle bulk, and making sure the sweep stays smoothly rounded through the joint bends while starting correctly embedded inside the body surface at the hip.

Checking the hip x-offset against the body's hip width, I'm adjusting so the leg socket sits flush rather than poking through—settling on hip x=0.14, knee 0.2, hock 0.18, paw 0.18 for the hind leg, and similarly tucking the foreleg x-offsets to about 0.14-0.15 to keep the wolf's chest narrow and shoulders properly tucked against the body.

Still refining body proportions...

The neck chain tapers from 0.16 down to 0.12 radius as it rises, with joint points plotting the forward curve up to the head socket. I'm positioning the skull center and head length so the neck tube end radius of 0.115 fits cleanly against the skull radius of 0.12.

Reconsidering the head height — raising it higher for an alert pose, pushing the final neck joint up to y=1.2 and adjusting the slope through the intermediate points. Checking total height against the 1.5m model scale: ears top out around 1.52, but the shoulder height from the spine's chest position plus its radius comes to roughly 1.17, which seems disproportionately tall compared to the leg length.

Scaling back the proportions — lowering the spine points and reducing the chest radius so shoulder height sits closer to 1.08, with the mane fur adding up to about 1.15. I'm adjusting the leg joints accordingly, placing shoulders around y=0.72 and elbows near 0.46, and recomputing the belly bottom to land around 0.58. Updating the spine path coordinates and the neck joints N0 through N2, then placing the head center around (0, 1.15, 0.84) to start defining the skull shape.

Setting the skull top near 1.27 with ears extending to 1.47 and the nose tip pushed forward to z=1.2, while thickening the neck ruff and tube at its base for a more muscular look. I'm working out the parent-child joint hierarchy — hips as root, hind legs attaching near z=-0.42, forelegs and neck both parenting off the third spine joint — and adding a shoulder muscle bulge as a scaled ellipsoid to give the forelimbs a chunkier, more stylized silhouette.

Now I'm adding a similar haunch bulge near the hip joint for the hind legs, then moving on to shaping the tail as a four-segment chain tapering from the hips, working out a sine-based radius function to get a bushy base that thins toward the tip.

Writing tail gradient and sweep code...

Now I'm planning fur tufts as cheap spike meshes, checking whether the spike function supports a sides option and how its signature handles direction versus tip arguments.

I'm picking a small flat color palette for the mane—grays and a cream tone—and deciding to scatter spikes across the neck surface with a minimum distance and a normal-based filter to control where tufts appear.

Now I'm working out spike orientation using each hit's normal blended with a backward-leaning direction, randomizing length and radius, and deciding whether to anchor spike bases directly at the surface hit or offset them slightly, weighing the tradeoff of losing bone binding against getting a smoother blend.

I'm planning the fur distribution: a chest ruff of cream spikes scattered on the front torso filtered by position and normal, pointing down and back, plus shoulder and back fur scattered more broadly, and a dorsal ridge running along the body tube's centerline using an along-sweep helper.

For the dorsal spikes and mane continuation along the neck, I'll compute direction vectors from the sweep normal blended with a backward-tilted vector, deciding to use the simpler scatter approach for the neck mane rather than the along-sweep method since the neck isn't horizontal. Now I'm moving to cheek ruff spikes positioned relative to the head's cheek offsets.

Writing muzzle details next...

Still working out head geometry...

Working out the lower jaw geometry so it tapers to a small gap near the tip, leaving room for teeth to show in a near-closed mouth with slight opening angle.

For the eyes, I'm placing them on the skull surface using azimuth/elevation around the skull's center so left and right mirror correctly, positioned slightly forward with amber color, then adding elongated brow shapes above each eye.

Now I'm working through paw geometry, computing toe positions as small spheres arranged along the x-axis near the paw tip for each leg.

Still defining leg joint positions...

I'm thinking I can skip dewclaws, but maybe add small fur tufts at the hock and elbow for extra detail—nothing too elaborate. The leg skin will smooth over the sharp joint bends and use the coat color, with front legs getting colored similarly.

For the eyes, I'll use the glow kit from the stick builder's kits, applying it to the eye parts with a warm amber color and moderate strength, keeping the material flat and unpainted so glow works correctly. I'm double-checking ground contact: paw bottoms sit right at y=0 with claws just above, and the tail tip clears the ground fine. I'm also considering adding a Warcraft-style touch like war-paint or a harness to the wolf for extra flavor.

I want to add some rugged details for a Blizzard-style look: a notched ear, scars, glowing eyes, torn fur, big claws, and maybe a scar across the muzzle or a faint chest patch, though some of these I may skip for simplicity. For facial markings, I'm painting a darker nose bridge using a smoothstep function based on proximity to the center line and height, applied in model space on the scaled sphere parts.

Now I'm writing a helper to interpolate radii values across a sequence of keyframes for lofting the body shape...

Working through the body radius and shift functions for the sweep -- the shift axis needs to align with the frame's local up so the body droops correctly along the spine chain, and I'm setting the sweep options to use smooth shading with varying polygon sides (10 for body/neck, 8 elsewhere) to get a painterly Warcraft-style look rather than faceted low-poly. Then I'm setting up the surface sweep itself for the scatter pass.

Now I'm setting up the imports and the color palette -- dark, mid, and light fur tones plus cream, tan, and dark accent colors. I'm writing the coat paint function that layers large-scale and fine-scale noise (scaled differently along axes to mimic fur streak direction) and blends between the fur colors using mix calls based on the noise values.

I'm adding a darker saddle region on the back using smoothstep based on normal and position, then a lighter belly/chest region using a vertical smoothstep gradient.

Adding muzzle cream tint and nose bridge darkening...

I'm making sure noise and color functions return proper types, avoiding unnecessary vector allocations, and now working out the tail's gradient blend from coat color to dark tip along its path.

Next I'm figuring out skull and jaw coloring, reusing the coat color for both, then moving to the ears—keeping the outer ear coat-colored while giving the inner ear a pinkish-cream tone, and sketching the ear outline shape.

Checking whether the outline type properly supports sharp-corner points for the pointed ear shape, and tracking down where to import the right type definition from.

Adjusting ear positioning offsets...

Now I'm computing the ear's orientation vector using a cross product of the thickness and length axes, checking the sign flips so the left and right ears mirror correctly along the z-axis.

Now I'm working out where the ear base should sit on the skull, computing the surface position at the given offset so the ear attaches at the right height and depth, slightly embedded into the head.

Setting the ear orientation to lean forward a bit instead of back for an alert pose, verifying the direction vectors stay orthogonal independent of the lean angle. Now I'm starting to write the build function for the wolf model.

Defining hips joint and spine chain...

Checking belly and chest heights against leg placement to confirm proportions line up, then starting the neck chain as a short curve rising forward from the spine end, with a tapering tube sweep for its shape.

Now I'm attaching the head joint to the end of the neck chain, defining its orientation, and setting up a local coordinate helper so I can position facial features relative to the head consistently rather than repeating raw coordinates everywhere.

Still writing skull geometry...

I'll skip flat shading mostly but enable it on the chunky low-poly parts like paws, toes, haunch, shoulder, and skull to show faceted bulk, confirming the part options support a flat:true flag for both spheres and sticks. Then I'm shaping the muzzle with a tapered frustum box between the head and nose, and adding fur bridging across the top of the muzzle.

Now I'm adding small facial details: a nose ellipsoid at the snout tip, skipping nostril detail and lip skirts for simplicity, and placing spike-shaped upper and lower canine teeth positioned near the jaw and head bones with ivory coloring.

Checking that upper canines sit laterally outside the lower jaw edge, confirms good fit. I'm adding a dark mouth interior box and a pink tongue mesh positioned near the jaw top, then moving on to define the jaw joint.

Now I'm setting up the lower jaw as a tapered frustum shape with cream coloring on the underside and gray fur coat on top, plus a chin tuft spike. Writing cheek ruff spike loop...

Placing eyes using a surface hit-test against the skull geometry, stamping small ellipsoid eye shapes with amber color, embedding and spinning them slightly, then adding a glow effect.

Still working out pupil placement math...

Now I'm adding brows with their own stick placement and spin, then moving on to building the neck mane using a scattered spike pattern across the neck surface.

For each mane spike, I'm varying color between the fur palette shades and computing the direction to flow backward and downward along the neck, blending the surface normal with a fixed back-down vector to get that swept mane look from head toward shoulders.

For tail tuft direction, since scattered hits lack tangent info, I'm approximating the backward/downward flow manually, adjusting more toward -z near the tail base where the curve bends back, and considering pulling the actual tangent from the tail path instead.

Using closestT and tangentAt on the path gives a usable direction for tuft orientation, combined with the normal — applying the same approach for the neck but reversed, and darkening the color near the tail tip. Now I'm sketching out the leg-building function, laying out front leg points per side and constructing the path.

Writing chain code...

Still building leg joints...

I'll skip the tilt and just center the ellipsoid without rotation, then add fur tufts at the hock and elbow using spike shapes angled backward. Now I'm defining the paw function starting with an ellipsoid part for the foot shape.

Finishing paw...

Setting the scatter's randomness seed, then tallying up the part counts across body, head, legs, and spike groups to make sure the total geometry stays reasonable — roughly 290 parts and around 4.5k triangles, which seems fine for performance.

I need a helper function to compute fur direction by blending a hit's normal with flow direction and normalizing, plus typing for the hit points coming out of the scatter function. I'm also adding a generic palette-picking helper that randomly selects an item from an array.

I should double-check for unused imports and parameters since strict TypeScript settings may flag them as errors—making sure everything I import (THREE, builder, catmull, rng, paint, mix, noise, smoothstep, gradient, glow) actually gets used, and skipping resolve/polyline/frame if they're not needed in the coat-building logic.

Now I'm verifying the mix function's signature works correctly for color blending, confirming the chain's "aim" requirement for the jaw, and building out the tail structure—defining a Catmull-Rom path for the tail vertebrae, chaining it off the hips with a tapering radius sweep from thick to thin along its length.

I'm settling on round-to-point end caps for the tail so the tip comes to a bushy point, checking that the final tip height still fits within the overall body proportions. I'm also setting up a gradient from the coat color to dark near the tail's end for a natural color fade, then moving on to building the skull part for the eyes using the part() function.

I need to guard against null hits when positioning things on the skull surface, confirm the eye glow effect works with the Part's mesh property, and finalize the ear geometry with extrusion, bevel, and inner coloring. I'm also double-checking the neck-to-head radius transitions and z-axis alignment between the head and chest before writing out the final code.

I considered adding a scar or notch detail but decided against it due to risk of floating geometry, and I'm skipping extra brow fur. Now I'm writing a keyframe interpolation helper function with smoothstep easing.

Still writing helper functions...

For the neck mane, I'll flow the hair backward along the neck direction with a downward droop added to simulate natural drape.

For body back tufts, I'm orienting them along the spine's z-tangent with a backward sign, while the chest ruff points down and back using a combined normal and offset vector. I'm checking that the sweep chain across neck joints and the separate head joint works correctly, and confirming ear base positions resolve to proper Vector3 points for extrusion.

Tooth spikes need explicit bone assignment since their base positions are computed without inherited bones. I'm skipping whisker details on the muzzle fur and finalizing the code now.
